title: Given a Scenario, Configure Microsoft Windows Networking Features on a Client/Desktop

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: A Windows client can join local or centralized environments, share resources, use static or dynamic IP configuration, establish several connection types, and apply network security profiles.
The main mental model is: identity → local access → IP configuration → connection type → security profile → network resources.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Can you identify whether a Windows networking scenario involves domain or workgroup membership, shared resources, IP settings, connection type, firewall, profile, proxy, network path, or data limits?
bullets: Drive letter to a share → mapped drive

sections.title: Domain Joined vs. Workgroup
paragraphs: A workgroup is decentralized: each computer manages its own users, passwords, permissions, and resources. A domain provides centralized authentication, accounts, Group Policy, and resource access.

entries.title: Shared Resources
paragraphs: Folders and other resources can be made available to authenticated network users subject to sharing and filesystem permissions.

entries.title: Printers
paragraphs: A printer may be shared from a computer, print server, or network-connected device for many users.

entries.title: File Servers
paragraphs: A file server centrally stores files accessed by network clients.

entries.title: Mapped Drives
paragraphs: A mapped drive assigns a drive letter such as Z: to a network path such as \\server\share.
entries.recognitionCue: A network folder appears as drive S: → mapped drive.

sections.title: Local OS Firewall Settings
paragraphs: Windows Defender Firewall filters endpoint traffic. Its configuration can vary across domain, private, and public profiles.

entries.title: Application Restrictions and Exceptions
paragraphs: Restrictions block an application's traffic; an exception permits the required application or traffic when appropriate.
entries.recognitionCue: An application works locally but its network traffic is blocked → configure a firewall exception.

entries.title: Configuration
paragraphs: Choose the correct profile, direction, protocol, port, and application scope rather than disabling the firewall broadly.

sections.title: Client Network Configuration

entries.title: Internet Protocol (IP) Addressing Scheme
paragraphs: The IP address identifies the client on the network.

entries.title: Domain Name System (DNS) Settings
paragraphs: DNS translates names into IP addresses.
entries.recognitionCue: IPs work but names fail → investigate DNS.

entries.title: Subnet Mask
paragraphs: The subnet mask identifies which addresses are local to the client.

entries.title: Gateway
paragraphs: The default gateway forwards traffic toward other networks.
entries.recognitionCue: The client cannot leave its local subnet → verify the gateway.

entries.title: Static vs. Dynamic
paragraphs: Static settings are manually assigned and remain until changed. Dynamic settings are automatically assigned, commonly by DHCP.
entries.memoryHook: Type it → static. Receive it → dynamic.

sections.callout: Address = who am I; mask = who is local; gateway = how do I leave; DNS = how do I find names.

entries.title: Virtual Private Network (VPN)
paragraphs: A VPN creates an encrypted logical tunnel across another network such as the Internet.
entries.recognitionCue: A remote employee securely connects to the company network → VPN.

entries.title: Wireless
paragraphs: A wireless client commonly uses Wi-Fi to join a local WLAN through an access point.

entries.title: Wired
paragraphs: A wired client commonly uses Ethernet cabling.

entries.title: Wireless Wide Area Network (WWAN)/Cellular Network
paragraphs: WWAN provides wide-area connectivity through a cellular carrier rather than a local Wi-Fi access point.
entries.recognitionCue: A laptop uses a carrier modem away from Wi-Fi → WWAN.

sections.title: Proxy Settings
paragraphs: A proxy is an intermediary between the client and a destination. Organizations use proxies for filtering, logging, access control, or policy enforcement.
sections.callout: Client → proxy → destination. A proxy is a middleman; a VPN is a secure tunnel.

sections.title: Public Network vs. Private Network
paragraphs: A public profile suits untrusted networks such as hotels, airports, and coffee shops and applies restrictive discovery and sharing behavior. A private profile suits a trusted home or office LAN.

sections.title: File Explorer Navigation—Network Paths
paragraphs: A Universal Naming Convention (UNC) path such as \\server\share directly identifies a network resource. A mapped drive assigns that path a local drive letter.
sections.callout: Network address → UNC path. Drive letter → mapped drive.

sections.title: Metered Connections and Limitations
paragraphs: A metered connection tells Windows that data is limited or costly. Windows may reduce update downloads, background synchronization, and application traffic.
sections.callout: A capped cellular plan → configure the connection as metered.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Drive letter to share → mapped drive

entries.title: Domain vs. Workgroup
paragraphs: Domain is centralized; workgroup is local and decentralized.

entries.title: Static vs. Dynamic
paragraphs: Static is manually assigned; dynamic is received automatically, commonly from DHCP.

entries.title: Gateway vs. DNS
paragraphs: Gateway reaches other networks; DNS resolves names.

entries.title: VPN vs. Proxy
paragraphs: VPN is an encrypted network tunnel; proxy is an intermediary for selected traffic.

entries.title: Wi-Fi vs. WWAN
paragraphs: Wi-Fi uses a local access point; WWAN uses a cellular provider.

entries.title: Mapped Drive vs. UNC Path
paragraphs: A mapped drive uses a drive letter; a UNC path directly names the network resource.
